title: Discovery of Bioresorbable Polymer Suture Coatings for Controlled Tissue Regeneration with Multimodal Foundation Models
summary: Therapeutic sutures can localize bioactive payloads to wounds, but burst release and insufficient coating durability can compromise regeneration and increase infection risk. In this work, we introduce a data-driven discovery strategy for bioresorbable polymer suture coatings that improve therapeutic retention and release kinetics. We develop GenPoly, an end-to-end multimodal generative framework that learns a shared polymer representation over paired polymer string sequences and molecular graphs via contrastive alignment, and couples this representation to property prediction, synthetic accessibility filtering, and motif-based candidate clustering to discover coating families beyond commonly used linear aliphatic polyesters. Starting from a clinically prevalent baseline, GenPoly identifies candidate coatings and selects representative polymers for experimental evaluation on nanoparticle-loaded sutures with recombinant human EGF to an in vitro human keratinocyte wound model. A discovered polymer coating of the LA-TMC family shows improved payload retention and sustained release, exhibiting a $3.3\times$ increase in rhEGF concentration, accompanied by more localized Ki-67-positive keratinocyte proliferation at the wound bed, in comparison with the current state-of-the-art candidates. These findings suggest new opportunities in AI-driven polymer discovery, and highlight the viability of GenPoly in engineering bioresorbable coatings for suture-based therapeutic delivery in targeted tissue regeneration.

AI.tldr: GenPoly, an end-to-end multimodal generative framework, discovers bioresorbable polymer suture coatings that improve therapeutic retention and release kinetics, identifying an LA-TMC family coating with 3.3x higher rhEGF concentration and enhanced localized keratinocyte proliferation.
AI.motivation: Therapeutic sutures can localize bioactive payloads to wounds, but burst release and insufficient coating durability compromise regeneration and increase infection risk. There is a need for improved bioresorbable polymer coatings with better therapeutic retention and release kinetics, going beyond commonly used linear aliphatic polyesters.
AI.method: GenPoly is an end-to-end multimodal generative framework that learns a shared polymer representation over paired polymer string sequences and molecular graphs via contrastive alignment. This representation is coupled to property prediction, synthetic accessibility filtering, and motif-based candidate clustering to discover new coating families. Starting from a clinically prevalent baseline, GenPoly identifies candidates and selects representative polymers for experimental evaluation on nanoparticle-loaded sutures with recombinant human EGF in an in vitro human keratinocyte wound model.
AI.result: A discovered polymer coating of the LA-TMC family shows improved payload retention and sustained release, exhibiting a 3.3x increase in rhEGF concentration, accompanied by more localized Ki-67-positive keratinocyte proliferation at the wound bed compared with current state-of-the-art candidates.
AI.conclusion: These findings suggest new opportunities in AI-driven polymer discovery and highlight the viability of GenPoly in engineering bioresorbable coatings for suture-based therapeutic delivery in targeted tissue regeneration.

title: Disease-level drug approval forecasting from trial-agnostic public data
summary: Drug development is an expensive and lengthy process requiring developers to select drugs for human trials and diseases to target. Computational tools that can estimate before testing which drug-disease candidates are most likely to reach FDA approval could reduce development time and costs through early program advancement and disease prioritization. Yet existing approaches predict outcomes at a single level or stage or do not distinguish between disease outcomes for the same drug. We ask (1) whether FDA approval can be forecast for a drug-disease pair using only pre-clinical trial information, and (2) whether these forecasts can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. We built a cohort of 14,134 drug-disease pairs by reconstructing programs from ClinicalTrials.gov, extracting disease-level approvals from FDA label documentation, and enriching each pair with molecular, disease, ADMET, target, and pathway features. We divided the cohort into pre- and post-2019 programs and trained a classifier on pre-2019 data to predict FDA approval. On the post-2019 cohort (2,637 programs), the model would have prioritized a program that ultimately gained approval over one that did not approximately three out of four times. For drugs tested across multiple diseases, selecting the model's highest-ranked disease would have identified an ultimately approved disease 61.3% of the time, compared with 40.7% under random selection. These results show that public pre-trial information contains signal for forecasting FDA approval at the drug-disease level and can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. We provide a public web tool for SMILES- and ICD-10-based drug-disease approval forecasting.

AI.tldr: A classifier trained on pre-2019 drug-disease pairs using pre-clinical features forecasts FDA approval on post-2019 programs (~75% pairwise accuracy) and helps prioritize diseases for the same drug (61.3% vs 40.7% random).
AI.motivation: Drug development is costly and lengthy, and developers must pick drugs for trials and diseases to target. Existing computational tools predict outcomes at a single level/stage or fail to distinguish disease outcomes for the same drug.
AI.method: Built a cohort of 14,134 drug-disease pairs from ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA labels, and molecular/disease/ADMET/target/pathway features. Split into pre-/post-2019 programs; trained a classifier on pre-2019 data to predict FDA approval.
AI.result: On 2,637 post-2019 programs, the model prioritized an ultimately approved program over a non-approved one ~3 of 4 times. For multi-disease drugs, the top-ranked disease was approved 61.3% of the time vs 40.7% random.
AI.conclusion: Public pre-trial information contains signal for forecasting FDA approval at the drug-disease level and can help prioritize diseases for the same drug. A public web tool enables SMILES- and ICD-10-based approval forecasting.

title: Energy, Information, and the Limits of Neuropsychiatric Classification
summary:
Importance: The search for reliable neuroimaging biomarkers of mental disorders has remained elusive despite decades of research. Why clinically consequential disorders yield weak neuroimaging separability remains unresolved. Drawing on statistical thermodynamics and the metabolic costs of neural coding, we propose that psychiatric disorders produce constrained deformations of a largely shared repertoire of brain activity patterns, limiting the class-specific information available for classification.
  Observations: We develop a framework linking physical resource constraints, landscape deformation, distributional separation, and attainable classification, and examine its components using human neuroimaging, synthetic data, and an exactly specified physical model. In resting-state fMRI from 1952 FOR2107 participants (823 with major depressive disorder; 1129 healthy controls), held-out energy-landscape estimates and nonlinear classifiers agreed across 13 comparisons (r = 0.996). Similar results emerged at both FOR2107 centers and in 900 SRPBS participants spanning multiple psychiatric diagnoses. In synthetic data, classification improved with distributional separation and approached the optimum. In an equilibrium three-well model, statistical energy equaled physical potential energy scaled by inverse temperature. Modest deformation redistributed state occupancy while optimal snapshot classification remained weak. A literature map found insufficiently comparable evidence to test the human metabolic constraint.
  Conclusions: Clinically consequential differences may arise within a largely shared neural repertoire. The thermodynamic framework connects physical deformation to classification under specified assumptions; its metabolic implementation in humans remains untested. Testing this mechanism requires joint measurements of brain activity, bodily physiology, and metabolism.

AI.tldr: Psychiatric disorders may only weakly deform a largely shared repertoire of brain activity patterns, so neuroimaging biomarkers stay weak. A thermodynamic framework linking metabolic constraints, energy-landscape deformation, and classifiability is supported by fMRI and model results, though the metabolic mechanism is untested in humans.
AI.motivation: Reliable neuroimaging biomarkers of mental disorders remain elusive, and it is unresolved why clinically meaningful disorders yield only weak neuroimaging separability despite decades of research.
AI.method: Drawing on statistical thermodynamics and metabolic costs of neural coding, the authors build a framework connecting resource constraints, landscape deformation, distributional separation, and attainable classification, testing it with resting-state fMRI (1952 FOR2107 participants, 900 SRPBS participants), synthetic data, and an equilibrium three-well physical model, plus a literature map.
AI.result: Held-out energy-landscape estimates and nonlinear classifiers agreed across 13 comparisons (r = 0.996); similar findings appeared across FOR2107 centers and SRPBS diagnoses. In synthetic data classification improved with distributional separation and approached optimum, and in the three-well model statistical energy equaled physical potential energy scaled by inverse temperature, with modest deformation shifting occupancy but leaving optimal snapshot classification weak. Literature evidence was insufficient to test the human metabolic constraint.
AI.conclusion: Clinically consequential differences may arise within a largely shared neural repertoire. The thermodynamic framework links physical deformation to classification under specified assumptions, but its metabolic implementation in humans remains untested and requires joint measurements of brain activity, bodily physiology, and metabolism.

title: Bayesian Uncertainty Quantification of Breast-Cancer Pathology AI Agreement under Reader- and Annotation-Condition-Dependent Reference Labels
comment: In Review with Journal of Medical Imaging
summary: Human reference labels used to evaluate medical AI can vary across readers and annotation workflows. We quantified agreement of a fixed pathology AI system with a future qualified reader without treating inferred consensus as error-free biological truth. Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data were analyzed using a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. The selected frame contained 1,144 anchors, 52 fields of view, five slides/patients, and five primary readers. The target was fixed-AI agreement with a future reader, with descriptive contrast $Δ=θ_E-θ_U$. Analyses included raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment. Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs observed in both conditions, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state, while raw agreement was 0.5466 in Unbiased and 0.5473 in Evaluation. The reader-only model gave $Δ=-0.0008$ (95% CrI, $-0.0033$ to $0.0008$), and the shared-detectability model gave $Δ\approx0$ ($-0.0140$ to $0.0127$). Across structural perturbations, absolute agreement ranged from 0.420 to 0.646 in Unbiased and 0.409 to 0.640 in Evaluation. Frozen adversarial simulations met the comparative-stability criterion (median $R=0.295$; 14/16 model-scenario cells had $R<1$). Held-out-AI prediction supported shared predictive information, but varied by slide composition. The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast was comparatively stable, whereas absolute agreement was structurally sensitive. These findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or new-patient transportability. Evaluations using variable human references should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.

AI.tldr: This study quantifies how well a fixed pathology AI system agrees with future qualified readers across two multirater datasets, finding that the Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast is stable (~0) while absolute agreement is structurally sensitive.
AI.motivation: Human reference labels for medical AI evaluation vary across readers and annotation workflows, so treating inferred consensus as error-free ground truth is problematic. A framework is needed to assess AI-reader agreement without assuming biological truth.
AI.method: Linked Evaluation and Unbiased NuCLS multirater data (1,144 anchors, 52 FOVs, 5 slides/patients, 5 readers) analyzed with a fixed external HoVer-Net decision vector. Used raw agreement and iMRMC benchmarks, reader-only and shared-detectability Bayesian models, structural sensitivities, adversarial simulations, and predictive assessment; contrast Δ=θ_E−θ_U.
AI.result: Among 5,188 reader-anchor pairs, 19.62% changed AI-agreement state; raw agreement 0.5466 (Unbiased) vs 0.5473 (Evaluation). Reader-only Δ=−0.0008 (95% CrI −0.0033 to 0.0008); shared-detectability Δ≈0 (−0.0140 to 0.0127). Absolute agreement varied (0.420–0.646 Unbiased; 0.409–0.640 Evaluation). Adversarial sims met stability criterion (median R=0.295; 14/16 cells R<1).
AI.conclusion: The Evaluation-minus-Unbiased contrast is comparatively stable, but absolute agreement is structurally sensitive. Findings do not establish equivalence, causal assistance effects, biological accuracy, or transportability. Variable-reference evaluations should report reader population, selected frame, observation mechanism, and structural sensitivity.

title: Amortised Global Sensitivity Analysis of Pharmacokinetic models for Simulated Clinical Trials
comment: 68 pages, 15 figures, 11 tables; main text followed by supplementary material. Code: https://github.com/DanielePessina/jaxgsa
summary: Pharmacokinetic and pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic models are used in simulated clinical trials to compare dosing protocols and patient groups before a trial is run. Distinct virtual patient cohorts, representing renal impairment, obesity and overdosage, can impose different input distributions on the same model. Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) identifies which uncertain inputs drive the cohort's predictions, but a direct analysis incurs its full computational cost for every cohort. An alternative accounting is proposed here: a single surrogate is trained on an input envelope wide enough to contain every cohort, each cohort is then analysed using that surrogate, and the reported quantity is the number of cohorts at which the surrogate route has cost fewer mechanistic evaluations than the direct route. The study tests three GSA methods: variance-based GSA, Morris screening and optimal transport. It covers four PK and PK/PD models with seven to twenty-three free inputs, 21 cohorts and five surrogates. Every estimate is scored against a converged mechanistic solution obtained with its own method, and all costs are expressed in mechanistic model evaluations. The parameter ranking is recovered at low cost: gradient-boosted trees reconstruct it on 20 of the 21 cohorts and cost fewer evaluations to train than one direct cohort analysis, on all four models, at break-even counts between 0.02 and 0.14 cohorts. Amortisation is fastest at the highest dimensions, where each direct variance-based sample of a $D$-input model requires $D+2$ evaluations while the training budget does not scale accordingly. Recovering absolute index values is harder, and fewer surrogates manage it as inputs grow: two of the five surrogates fail at fifteen inputs, where the gradient-boosted trees and the Gaussian process still succeed, and at twenty-three inputs no surrogate succeeds on a majority of cohorts.

AI.tldr: A single wide-envelope surrogate can amortise global sensitivity analysis across multiple virtual patient cohorts in PK/PK-PD models, recovering parameter rankings on 20/21 cohorts at a fraction of the cost of direct mechanistic analysis.
AI.motivation: Comparing dosing protocols and patient groups via simulated clinical trials is computationally expensive when distinct virtual cohorts (renal impairment, obesity, overdosage) each impose different input distributions on the same model. Global sensitivity analysis (GSA) is needed to identify which uncertain inputs drive predictions, but running GSA directly incurs its full cost for every cohort.
AI.method: A single surrogate is trained on an input envelope wide enough to contain all cohorts, then each cohort is analysed using that surrogate. The reported metric is the number of cohorts at which the surrogate route costs fewer mechanistic evaluations than the direct route. Three GSA methods (variance-based GSA, Morris screening, optimal transport) are tested across four PK and PK/PD models with 7-23 free inputs, 21 cohorts, and five surrogate types. All estimates are scored against converged mechanistic solutions, with costs expressed in mechanistic model evaluations.
AI.result: Parameter ranking is recovered at low cost: gradient-boosted trees reconstruct it on 20 of 21 cohorts and cost fewer evaluations to train than one direct cohort analysis on all four models, with break-even counts of 0.02-0.14 cohorts. Amortisation is fastest at the highest dimensions, since each direct variance-based sample of a D-input model requires D+2 evaluations while the training budget does not scale accordingly. Recovering absolute index values is harder: two of five surrogates fail at 15 inputs (Gradient-boosted trees and Gaussian process still succeed), and at 23 inputs no surrogate succeeds on a majority of cohorts.
AI.conclusion: A single surrogate trained on a cohort-encompassing input envelope provides an efficient amortised accounting for GSA, reliably recovering parameter rankings cheaply but struggling to recover absolute sensitivity index values as input dimensionality grows, especially beyond 23 inputs.

title: Multilateral governance of invasive alien species management: An ecological-economic model with Allee effect
summary: Invasive alien species (IAS) generate substantial ecological and economic damages that often transcend political boundaries, creating strong incentives for coordinated management. We develop a two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control that integrates prevention and eradication measures with population dynamics characterized by logistic growth and an Allee effect. We derive analytical results on the interaction between ecological thresholds and strategic behaviour and compare outcomes under cooperation (central planner) and non-cooperation (open loop Nash equilibrium and Markovian Nash equilibrium). We show that, under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication can eliminate invasive populations in finite time, and complete prevention of cross-border spread is generally not optimal. In the absence of an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable, implying long-run persistence of the invasive species. By contrast, the presence of an Allee effect fundamentally alters system dynamics by making extinction locally stable and creating a basin of attraction within which eradication becomes feasible. This finding highlights the economic significance of ecological thresholds and demonstrates how delays in management can shift populations beyond critical levels, after which eradication is unlikely regardless of subsequent control efforts. Numerical simulations further show that cooperative management expands the set of initial conditions leading to eradication and consistently reduces aggregate social costs relative to decentralized management. The results provide a formal rationale for rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, particularly in jurisdictions such as the European Union where listing and control actions may be delayed pending evidence of harm.

AI.tldr: A two-region ecological-economic model shows that Allee effects create a stable extinction basin enabling feasible eradication, and cooperation expands it while cutting social costs.
AI.motivation: Invasive alien species cause cross-border ecological and economic damages, creating incentives for coordinated control. The paper examines how ecological thresholds (Allee effects) interact with strategic behaviour under cooperation versus non-cooperation to inform prevention and eradication policy.
AI.method: Two-region ecological-economic model of IAS control integrating prevention and eradication with logistic growth and an Allee effect. Analytical derivation of ecological threshold–strategic behaviour interaction, comparing a central planner (cooperation) against open-loop and Markovian Nash equilibria (non-cooperation), supported by numerical simulations.
AI.result: Under realistic control costs, neither prevention nor eradication eliminates invasive populations in finite time, and full prevention of cross-border spread is generally suboptimal. Without an Allee effect, the zero-population equilibrium is unstable (long-run persistence). With an Allee effect, extinction becomes locally stable, creating a basin of attraction where eradication is feasible; delays can push populations past critical thresholds. Cooperation expands the eradication set of initial conditions and reduces aggregate social costs.
AI.conclusion: Ecological thresholds have significant economic meaning. The results justify rapid intervention, precautionary regulation, and stronger multilateral cooperation in IAS management, especially where listing and control actions are delayed pending evidence of harm (e.g., the European Union).

title: Full Lyapunov Spectra of Random Neural Networks, Part I: Finite-Time and Asymptotic Theory
summary: We develop a dynamical mean-field framework for the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks. At finite observation time, an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values leads to a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation yields an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and the repeated action of quenched connectivity. Direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra support the predictions in the regimes examined, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation also recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay illustrates how temporal correlations redistribute instability. This work was carried out in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol. Toward the end of preparation we became aware of David G. Clark's contemporaneous work, \emph{Lyapunov spectrum of random neural networks}[arXiv:2610.12426], which reports overlapping mean-field results for the full Lyapunov spectrum using a cavity approach.

AI.tldr: A dynamical mean-field framework is developed to compute the full finite-time and stationary asymptotic Lyapunov spectra of random recurrent neural networks, verified against direct singular-value and QR calculations.
AI.motivation: Understanding the full Lyapunov spectrum of random recurrent neural networks is important for characterizing their dynamics, yet a mean-field treatment covering both finite-time and stationary regimes while retaining local gain histories and quenched connectivity was lacking.
AI.method: The authors develop a dynamical mean-field framework. At finite observation time, they use an exact log-determinant representation of tangent-propagator singular values, yielding a closed-contour matrix Dyson equation for the smoothed spectral tail. In the stationary setting, a cocycle representation gives an operator equation for the asymptotic cumulative spectrum. Both formulations retain complete local gain histories and repeated action of quenched connectivity.
AI.result: Predictions are supported by direct singular-value calculations and network QR spectra in the examined regimes, with sampling uncertainty and numerical cutoffs assessed separately. The stationary equation recovers the known maximal exponent, and controlled gain-history replay shows how temporal correlations redistribute instability.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a unified mean-field description of finite-time and stationary Lyapunov spectra. The work was done in collaboration with ChatGPT 5.6 Sol, and it independently overlaps with contemporaneous cavity-approach results by David G. Clark.

title: A mathematical model for fitness effects on viral persistence
summary: Persistent viral infections arise from complex interactions between viral replication, host cell responses, and ongoing viral evolution. A general framework linking viral fitness to persistence dynamics is lacking. Here, we develop for the first time a mathematical model of viral persistence that takes into consideration viral fitness variations. Essential to the model is the partition of the classical fitness parameter into three components: replicative, infective, and dispersal fitness. The model was initially inspired by a new experiment on hepatitis C virus (HCV) persistence, established in human hepatoma cells, also reported in this work. This experiment documents two strikingly different viral trajectories depending on the initial replicative fitness of the viral population used to establish persistence. The dynamical model describes the interactions among uninfected cells, infected cells, and infectious virions, and it incorporates, through a continuum, two alternative mechanisms of viral release from cells: budding and lysis. Analysis of the model reveals that viral fitness parameters organise infection outcomes into distinct dynamical regimes. Low replicative and dispersal fitness values lead to viral extinction, whereas high values enable persistence through either stable coexistence or recurrent infection waves. The space of fitness discloses a hierarchy among these parameters, with replicative and dispersal fitness being able to trigger important shifts in the outcome of the infection as opposed to infective fitness. The model identifies trade-offs between replication and dispersal that shape viral production and predicts slow dynamical regimes in which infection may persist despite low detectable viral loads. It provide candidates mechanisms capable of generating the persistence patterns observed experimentally.

AI.tldr: A new mathematical model of viral persistence incorporating three fitness components (replicative, infective, dispersal) explains distinct infection outcomes, inspired by a new HCV persistence experiment.
AI.motivation: Persistent viral infections involve complex interactions between replication, host responses, and viral evolution, yet a general framework linking viral fitness to persistence dynamics is lacking.
AI.method: Develops a mathematical model partitioning the classical fitness parameter into replicative, infective, and dispersal components. It describes interactions among uninfected cells, infected cells, and virions, incorporating budding and lysis as viral release mechanisms. Inspired by a novel HCV persistence experiment in human hepatoma cells.
AI.result: Viral fitness parameters organize infection outcomes into distinct dynamical regimes: low replicative/dispersal fitness leads to extinction, while high values enable persistence via stable coexistence or recurrent infection waves. A fitness hierarchy emerges, with replicative and dispersal fitness driving outcome shifts unlike infective fitness. Trade-offs between replication and dispersal shape viral production, and slow regimes allow persistence despite low viral loads.
AI.conclusion: The model provides candidate mechanisms generating experimentally observed persistence patterns and offers a general framework linking viral fitness to persistence dynamics.

title: Ensemble-Based Modelling of Optogenetic Bioprocesses under Phototoxicity
summary: Optogenetics enables methanol-free protein production in the yeast $\textit{Komagataella phaffii}$ using light as a control input, facilitated by the blue-light-responsive transcription factor EL222. This opens the door to more programmable protein production in the food and biopharmaceutical industries. However, excessive illumination can inhibit growth and protein accumulation in some of these engineered cell factories. Previous hybrid modelling used black-box regression across sparsely sampled conditions to infer light-dependent kinetic parameters, without explicitly representing intracellular regulation. Here, we develop a multiscale mechanistic model linking EL222 activation, transcription, and translation to protein, biomass, and substrate dynamics. A latent light-associated stress state represents photoinhibitory effects on growth, transcription, and translation. An ensemble-based parameter-estimation strategy combines repeated global-local optimisation with screening for parameter sets supporting locally stable intracellular steady states under specified light conditions. Using available batch data for yeast-enhanced green fluorescent protein production in a $\textit{K. phaffii}$ strain carrying eight EL222 gene copies, the ensemble-mean predictions captured the main experimental trends in protein accumulation and growth across six constant light intensities. Parameter variability was propagated to time-course predictions, providing an empirical assessment of parameter-related uncertainty. Wider prediction bands coincided with less complete experimental coverage of the growth phases. Overall, the framework provides a mechanistic basis for future model-based optimisation and control of optogenetic bioprocesses under phototoxicity.

AI.tldr: A multiscale mechanistic model links EL222 photoactivation, transcription, and translation to protein/biomass/substrate dynamics in optogenetic K. phaffii, using an ensemble parameter-estimation strategy to predict growth and protein production across light intensities.
AI.motivation: Optogenetics enables methanol-free, light-controlled protein production in K. phaffii via the blue-light-responsive EL222 transcription factor, benefiting food and biopharmaceutical industries. However, excessive illumination inhibits growth and protein accumulation. Prior hybrid models used black-box regression over sparse conditions without explicitly representing intracellular regulation, motivating a more mechanistic approach.
AI.method: The authors developed a multiscale mechanistic model connecting EL222 activation, transcription, and translation to protein, biomass, and substrate dynamics. A latent light-associated stress state captures photoinhibitory effects. An ensemble-based parameter-estimation strategy combines repeated global-local optimisation with screening for parameter sets yielding locally stable intracellular steady states under given light conditions.
AI.result: Using batch data for enhanced green fluorescent protein production in a strain with eight EL222 gene copies, ensemble-mean predictions captured main experimental trends in protein accumulation and growth across six constant light intensities. Parameter variability was propagated to time-course predictions, giving an empirical uncertainty assessment; wider prediction bands aligned with less complete experimental coverage of growth phases.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a mechanistic basis for future model-based optimisation and control of optogenetic bioprocesses under phototoxicity.

title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
summary: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

AI.tldr: This paper trains an EEG encoder to align single-channel anterior-posterior differential signals with semantic embeddings of task instructions, stimuli, and response demands, enabling zero-shot and few-shot cognitive-state decoding across heterogeneous public datasets.
AI.motivation: EEG and noninvasive recordings could let simple wearables reveal cognitive states, but public EEG data are hard to combine because labs use different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised EEG representations have not consistently decoded cognitive state well, so task information needed to be incorporated.
AI.method: Experimental instructions, stimuli, and response demands were embedded in a common semantic space. An EEG encoder was trained to align signals from a single anterior-posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction with labeled samples.
AI.result: On a reserved ten-class evaluation, best zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% with 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own recording. Training on datasets with multiple tasks per participant helped, while adding single- or few-task datasets sometimes reduced performance despite broader task coverage.
AI.conclusion: These exploratory results suggest EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices, and independent studies would be especially useful for training an EEG foundation model to predict cognitive states.

title: Effective transport statistics for cooperative molecular motor ensembles with tether slack
summary: We improve upon our previous work using asymptotic analysis to characterize analytically the effective transport properties of a stochastic model for an ensemble of a cargo being pulled by two molecular motors walking on a microtubule. The governing equations are a system of stochastic differential equations with stochastic switching due to attachment and detachment kinetics of the molecular motors from the microtubule. Our model adopts a nonlinear tether which exerts no force when end-to-end distances are sufficiently small. This challenges some of the scale separation arguments from our previous work, and we modify the asymptotic analysis accordingly. In particular, spatial dynamics of the molecular motors may not always reach their quasi-stationary distribution within a particular attachment state. Rather, molecular motors tend to have a slack connection to the cargo for a while after they reattach, and we incorporate some first passage time analysis to determine if the tether becomes taut again. Through these and other modifications to the asymptotic analysis argument, the theoretical statistics for the run length, run time, and velocity of the motor-cargo ensemble can be brought into reasonable agreement with direct model simulations of two-motor ensembles consisting of kinesin-1 and kinesin-2. Additionally, we propose a new data fitting approach to obtain a double-exponential parameterization for the detachment rate of a motor as a function of the momentary force on its tether to the cargo, which is continuous at low load. Such a modified parameterization is needed to avoid artifacts in theoretical modeling of intracellular transport.

AI.tldr: Refines asymptotic analysis for effective transport of cargo pulled by two molecular motors, adding nonlinear (slack) tether and first-passage-time treatment; theory now matches simulations for kinesin-1/kinesin-2 ensembles, plus a new double-exponential detachment-rate fitting approach.
AI.motivation: Previous asymptotic work assumed scale separation and quasi-stationary motor dynamics, but a nonlinear tether that exerts no force at small end-to-end distances invalidates these assumptions, since motors often remain slackly connected after reattachment.
AI.method: Analytically characterize effective transport properties of an SDE model with stochastic attachment/detachment switching. Modify asymptotic analysis: allow that motor spatial dynamics may not reach quasi-stationary distribution within a state, and use first-passage-time analysis to determine when the tether becomes taut again. Also propose a double-exponential parameterization for force-dependent detachment rate, continuous at low load.
AI.result: Theoretical statistics for run length, run time, and velocity show reasonable agreement with direct simulations of two-motor ensembles of kinesin-1 and kinesin-2. The new detachment-rate parameterization avoids artifacts in intracellular transport modeling.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating tether slackness via first-passage-time analysis fixes the breakdown of scale separation, yielding accurate analytic transport statistics and a better-behaved detachment-rate model for motor-cargo ensembles.

title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
comment: Accepted by Asia Pacific Bioinformatics Conference (APBC) 2026
summary: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity. This framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals.

AI.tldr: This paper presents an uncertainty-aware workflow linking dynamic deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) to genome-scale metabolic models via soft flux constraints, applied to muscles of control and high-fat diet mice.
AI.motivation: Glucose-derived labeling measured by DMI in vivo is noisy, making network-level metabolic interpretation difficult. There is a need to integrate noninvasive tracer imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling while accounting for measurement uncertainty and avoiding overclaiming from poorly identified signals.
AI.method: After [6,6'-2H2]glucose injection, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and HFD mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and uncertainty. Only reliable DMI quantities (glucose processing to hexokinase flux; oxidative entry to pyruvate dehydrogenase flux) were used as GEM anchors via two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties.
AI.result: Constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD changes were muscle-specific: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, while gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity.
AI.conclusion: The framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals, enabling uncertainty-aware, muscle-specific metabolic interpretation.

title: Homogeneity and heterogeneity of functional element composition of genome units across human and seven model organisms
summary:
Is a chromosome a miniature of its genome, with the same mix of functional elements as the whole? We ask this of eight annotated genomes: human, mouse, zebrafish, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila melanogaster, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Arabidopsis thaliana and maize. Elements are classified in a four-level hierarchy, from five major classes (protein-coding genes, ncRNA genes, transposable elements (TEs), pseudogenes, IG/TR gene segments) down to finer classes. Units are chromosomes or arms, cytogenetic bands, equal cuts of each chromosome, and random segments of matching size. We compare each unit with the genome and with other units, call compositions homogeneous when they differ by less than 5%, and score each against a random sample of the same size.
  The first finding is a surprising homogeneity. The level-1 compositions of the major chromosomes match each other and the genome in maize, zebrafish, yeast and C. elegans, and in fly down to the major arms. Finer classes can be homogeneous too: protein function in Arabidopsis, and the Wicker TE orders in maize. Enzyme reaction classes are interchangeable between chromosomes in all eight genomes.
  The second finding is a structured heterogeneity. Where a unit departs from its genome, it does so in one of three ways: clusters of named elements, such as rRNA genes or immune receptor loci; megabase-scale compartments, such as TE-rich pericentromeric heterochromatin; and lineage-specific gene families, visible only at the finest levels.
  Corrected for chance, the genomes fall into groups. For protein function and gene families, composition is more uniform in plants and fly than in vertebrates, and least uniform in C. elegans. For the major classes and TE orders, uniformity follows where each genome places its repeats, along the arms (maize, zebrafish) or around the centromeres (Arabidopsis, fly), not its lineage.

AI.tldr: Across eight annotated genomes, chromosome compositions largely mirror the whole genome (homogeneous), except for three recurring forms of structured heterogeneity; genome grouping depends on element class and repeat placement rather than lineage.
AI.motivation: The paper asks whether a chromosome is a miniature of its genome, sharing the same mix of functional elements. It tests this question comparatively across eight annotated genomes to determine when chromosomal composition is homogeneous versus structured.
AI.method: Elements were classified in a four-level hierarchy, from five major classes (protein-coding genes, ncRNA genes, transposable elements, pseudogenes, IG/TR gene segments) to finer classes. Units analyzed included chromosomes or arms, cytogenetic bands, equal cuts of each chromosome, and random segments of matching size. Each unit was compared with the genome and other units; compositions differing by less than 5% were called homogeneous, and each was scored against a random sample of the same size.
AI.result: Two main findings: (1) surprising homogeneity, with level-1 compositions matching across major chromosomes and the genome in maize, zebrafish, yeast, and C. elegans, and in fly down to major arms; finer classes can also be homogeneous (protein function in Arabidopsis, Wicker TE orders in maize), and enzyme reaction classes are interchangeable across all eight genomes. (2) Structured heterogeneity, where departures occur via clusters of named elements (e.g., rRNA genes, immune receptor loci), megabase-scale compartments (e.g., TE-rich pericentromeric heterochromatin), and lineage-specific gene families visible only at the finest levels. After correcting for chance, genomes group by composition: protein function and gene families are more uniform in plants and fly than vertebrates, least in C. elegans; for major classes and TE orders, uniformity follows repeat placement (arms in maize/zebrafish vs. centromeres in Arabidopsis/fly), not lineage.
AI.conclusion: Chromosomes are largely miniature versions of their genomes, but homogeneity is punctuated by structured heterogeneity in three forms. Genome grouping is driven by element class and where repeats are placed, rather than by lineage.

title: Data-Driven Discovery of a Hyperelastic Strain-Energy Function for Veins Using Constitutive Artificial Neural Networks
summary: Veins are commonly subjected to altered mechanical loading in clinical settings such as vein grafting, arteriovenous fistula creation, and tissue-engineered vascular graft implantation, making accurate constitutive models of venous tissue clinically important. Venous mechanical behavior differs characteristically from that of arteries, and existing constitutive models struggle to simultaneously fit the circumferential and axial stress-stretch responses across vein types. Here, we present a constitutive artificial neural network (CANN) framework that discovers a compact, interpretable hyperelastic constitutive model from biaxial mechanical data across three types of veins (saphenous, jugular, and inferior vena cava). The framework incorporates an expanded candidate function library with structurally motivated terms representing progressive fiber recruitment and fiber-family interactions. Sobol sensitivity analysis, correlation-based pruning, and response-level family collapse were then used to reduce the discovered basis to a compact strain-energy density function (SEF). The resulting eight-term SEF achieved significantly higher fitting accuracy than established venous constitutive models across all three types of veins $(R^2>0.9, p<0.01)$. These findings establish a framework for constitutive model discovery in veins and propose a candidate constitutive form for further validation across larger, independent cohorts.

AI.tldr: A constitutive artificial neural network (CANN) discovers a compact, interpretable hyperelastic model of venous tissue from biaxial data across three vein types, yielding an eight-term strain-energy function that outperforms established models.
AI.motivation: Veins undergo altered mechanical loading in procedures like vein grafting, arteriovenous fistula creation, and tissue-engineered graft implantation, so accurate constitutive models matter clinically. Venous behavior differs from arteries, and existing models cannot simultaneously fit circumferential and axial stress-stretch responses across vein types.
AI.method: A CANN framework discovers a compact hyperelastic model from biaxial mechanical data of saphenous, jugular, and inferior vena cava veins. It uses an expanded candidate function library with structurally motivated terms for progressive fiber recruitment and fiber-family interactions, reduced via Sobol sensitivity analysis, correlation-based pruning, and response-level family collapse to a compact strain-energy density function.
AI.result: The resulting eight-term strain-energy function achieved significantly higher fitting accuracy than established venous constitutive models across all three vein types (R²>0.9, p<0.01).
AI.conclusion: The work establishes a framework for constitutive model discovery in veins and proposes a candidate constitutive form for validation in larger, independent cohorts.

title: Simple model of neurogliovascular unit activity with noradrenaline leading force
summary: In this work we present a model of a neuroglivascular unit associated with a neuronal ensemble. We combine calcium dynamics in the astrocyte, the cascade of synthesis of arachidonic acid and its derivatives, as well as the activity of the network of inhibitory and excitatory neurons with changes in local blood flow. We add equations to the model for extracellular neurotransmitters such as GABA, glutamate, and norepinephrine. We show that the resulting model can exhibit different types of behavior, and also shows a significant connection between the functioning of the neural network and its supporting components.

AI.tldr: The authors build a model of a neurogliovascular unit linked to a neuronal ensemble, coupling astrocyte calcium dynamics, arachidonic acid synthesis, excitatory/inhibitory network activity, and local blood flow, plus extracellular GABA, glutamate, and norepinephrine equations, showing diverse behaviors and strong neural-support coupling.
AI.motivation: To understand how neuronal network activity interacts with its supporting glial and vascular components (neurogliovascular coupling).
AI.method: A mathematical model combining astrocyte calcium dynamics, arachidonic acid cascade, excitatory/inhibitory neuronal network activity, local blood flow, with added equations for extracellular GABA, glutamate, and norepinephrine.
AI.result: The model exhibits different types of behavior and reveals a significant connection between neural network functioning and its supporting components.
AI.conclusion: The integrated neurogliovascular-neuronal model captures rich dynamics and highlights tight coupling between neural activity and glial/vascular support.

title: Temporal invariance of evolutionary entropy and comparative demographic analysis
summary: Does evolutionary entropy depend on the width of the age classes used to describe a population? We show that the apparent dependence on temporal resolution is a consequence of the loss of information about reproductive timing within discrete classes. When this information is retained, corresponding continuous and discrete representations yield the same cycle entropy, generation time, evolutionary entropy, and reproductive potential in a common unit of time. When within-class timing is unknown, a uniform local reconstruction yields a logarithmic correction. For constant post-maturity hazard and fertility, continuous exponential and discrete geometric descriptions correspond exactly at every time scale. Thus, for a fixed reference duration, evolutionary entropy is a property of the reproductive process, not of its temporal partition. These results provide a mathematical basis for comparing demographic models across different temporal scales by identifying the information required to separate differences in reproductive organisation from effects of the chosen age-class representation.

AI.tldr: Evolutionary entropy is a property of the reproductive process, not of the temporal partitioning of age classes; apparent dependence on age-class width stems from loss of within-class timing information.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether evolutionary entropy depends on the width of age classes used to describe a population, which complicates comparisons of demographic models across temporal scales.
AI.method: The authors compare continuous and discrete demographic representations, retaining information about reproductive timing within discrete classes versus using a uniform local reconstruction when within-class timing is unknown, and derive corrections (logarithmic) accordingly. They test exact correspondence for constant post-maturity hazard and fertility (continuous exponential vs. discrete geometric).
AI.result: When within-class timing information is retained, continuous and discrete representations yield identical cycle entropy, generation time, evolutionary entropy, and reproductive potential in a common time unit. When within-class timing is unknown, a uniform local reconstruction gives a logarithmic correction. Continuous exponential and discrete geometric descriptions correspond exactly at every time scale.
AI.conclusion: For a fixed reference duration, evolutionary entropy is intrinsic to the reproductive process rather than its temporal partition, providing a mathematical basis for comparing demographic models across temporal scales and separating reproductive organisation from age-class representation effects.

title: A Robust Numerical Framework for Multi-Strain Epidemics
summary: Epidemiological models often take the form of systems of differential equations of varying levels of complexity. In multi-strain models, complexity arises from the interaction of diverse pathogen types that may exhibit different patterns of cross-immunity due to the host's immune system. Where previous work has tended to focus on theoretical analysis of this complexity, or model simplification, less effort has been given to efficient numerical exploration of full multi-strain disease dynamics. Here, we propose a computational framework for representing multi-strain disease transmission models, through a mathematically transparent hard-coded mapping between sets and integers. By mapping infection histories into Boolean matrices, the framework eliminates explicit iteration over strain combinations while preserving key biological processes, including sequential infection and partial cross-immunity. Benchmark comparisons of numerical solutions of our matrix formulation and a set-indexed implementation demonstrate substantial performance gains. Across models with increasing numbers of strains, the matrix formulation consistently reduces runtime, with a speedup exceeding two orders of magnitude for systems with 11 strains. We present an application of this approach to the case of COVID-19 in Indonesia, focusing on the replacement of the Delta variant by Omicron. We hope that our approach represents a robust computational approach to automatically generate diverse multi-strain epidemic models that can be solved in a computationally efficient manner for a variety of scientific and public-health questions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a computational framework that maps multi-strain infection histories to Boolean matrices, enabling efficient numerical solution of multi-strain epidemic models without explicit iteration over strain combinations.
AI.motivation: Multi-strain epidemiological models are complex due to interactions among diverse pathogen types with varying cross-immunity patterns. Prior work focused on theoretical analysis or model simplification, with less effort on efficient numerical exploration of full multi-strain disease dynamics.
AI.method: A hard-coded, mathematically transparent mapping between sets and integers is used. Infection histories are represented as Boolean matrices, eliminating explicit iteration over strain combinations while preserving key biological processes such as sequential infection and partial cross-immunity.
AI.result: Benchmark comparisons of the matrix formulation versus a set-indexed implementation show substantial performance gains. Runtime consistently decreases with increasing strains, achieving over two orders of magnitude speedup for systems with 11 strains. An application to COVID-19 in Indonesia examines Delta-to-Omicron variant replacement.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers a robust computational method to automatically generate diverse multi-strain epidemic models that can be solved efficiently for various scientific and public-health questions.

title: SIGHT: A Methodological Appraisal Framework for Evaluating Large Language Models in Ophthalmology
comment: 66 pages, 8 figures, 1 table. SIGHT appraisal framework (5 domains, 20 items)
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated across ophthalmic tasks, yet the methodological quality of these evaluations has received little attention. Most studies report accuracy while overlooking design features required for valid and clinically meaningful inference. We critically reviewed published ophthalmic LLM evaluation studies covering knowledge assessment, patient education, diagnostic reasoning, triage, clinical documentation, multimodal image interpretation, and uncertainty estimation. We used the methodological weaknesses that recurred across study designs to develop the SIGHT framework, which has five domains: Sample and item provenance, Independence and blinding, Ground truth and comparator fairness, Handling of paired and repeated-measures data, and Transparency and trustworthiness. Current evaluations rely heavily on benchmark accuracy, synthetic clinical vignettes, and curated datasets, and real-world clinical validation remains rare. Common limitations include potential training-data contamination, inadequate handling of paired data, limited assessment of inter-rater reliability, inconsistent reference standards, insufficient evaluation of calibration and uncertainty, and frequent overinterpretation of benchmark performance as evidence of clinical readiness. SIGHT provides twenty structured appraisal items to evaluate internal validity, interpretability, and applicability across diverse ophthalmic LLM study designs. It offers a practical way to appraise ophthalmic LLM studies and may improve the methodological quality, interpretability, and clinical relevance of future evaluations.

AI.tldr: The paper critically reviews ophthalmic LLM evaluation studies and proposes the SIGHT framework, a five-domain appraisal tool with twenty structured items to improve methodological quality and clinical relevance of these evaluations.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly evaluated across ophthalmic tasks, but most studies report only accuracy while neglecting design features needed for valid, clinically meaningful inference. The methodological quality of these evaluations has received little attention.
AI.method: The authors critically reviewed published ophthalmic LLM evaluation studies spanning knowledge assessment, patient education, diagnostic reasoning, triage, clinical documentation, multimodal image interpretation, and uncertainty estimation. From recurring methodological weaknesses, they developed the SIGHT framework with five domains: Sample and item provenance, Independence and blinding, Ground truth and comparator fairness, Handling of paired and repeated-measures data, and Transparency and trustworthiness.
AI.result: Current evaluations rely heavily on benchmark accuracy, synthetic clinical vignettes, and curated datasets, with real-world clinical validation remaining rare. Common limitations include training-data contamination, inadequate handling of paired data, limited inter-rater reliability assessment, inconsistent reference standards, insufficient calibration/uncertainty evaluation, and overinterpretation of benchmark performance as clinical readiness. SIGHT provides twenty structured appraisal items.
AI.conclusion: SIGHT offers a practical way to appraise ophthalmic LLM studies across diverse designs, evaluating internal validity, interpretability, and applicability, and may improve the methodological quality, interpretability, and clinical relevance of future evaluations.

title: CloneOT: predicting clone-specific perturbation responses with lineage-supervised neural inverse optimal transport
summary: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping between two unpaired populations of cells measured before and after the perturbation. Optimal transport (OT) provides a principled framework for constructing such mappings by minimizing the transport cost, and neural OT methods (\textit{e.g.}, CellOT) have been employed for this prediction task. However, these methods rely on a fixed transport cost, typically the squared Euclidean distance. This cost may connect cells with the wrong responses. Lineage tracing provides the information needed to learn the cost, as heritable barcodes link the cells of the same clone before and after the perturbation. Here, we propose \CloneOT, a neural inverse OT method that learns both the transport cost and the transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. \CloneOT\ represents the cost as a neural network. It learns the cost by minimizing the extra cost that the lineage adds to the optimal transport, so that the cheapest transport keeps the cells of each clone together. Our experiments demonstrate that \CloneOT\ recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets, while the squared Euclidean cost fails. Moreover, \CloneOT\ outperforms five baselines on 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios of cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. Furthermore, we show that \CloneOT\ reveals the clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts the fate of each clone from its cells before treatment. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/CloneOT.

AI.tldr: CloneOT is a neural inverse optimal transport method that learns both the transport cost and map from partially lineage-traced single-cell data, improving prediction of perturbation responses.
AI.motivation: Predicting single-cell perturbation responses requires mapping unpaired pre- and post-perturbation cell populations. Existing neural OT methods (e.g., CellOT) use a fixed transport cost like squared Euclidean distance, which can incorrectly match cells. Lineage tracing, where heritable barcodes link cells of the same clone across time, provides the information needed to learn a better cost.
AI.method: CloneOT is a neural inverse OT method that jointly learns the transport cost and transport map from partially lineage-traced single-cell datasets. The cost is represented as a neural network and learned by minimizing the extra cost that lineage information adds to the optimal transport, so the cheapest transport keeps clone cells together.
AI.result: CloneOT recovers the correct transport on 2D datasets where squared Euclidean cost fails. It outperforms five baselines across 14 lineage-tracing perturbation scenarios in cancer cells, for both seen and unseen clones. It also reveals clone-specific transcriptional programs of drug-tolerant persister cells and forecasts each clone's fate from pre-treatment cells.
AI.conclusion: Learnable, lineage-informed transport costs substantially improve OT-based prediction of single-cell perturbation responses, offering biological insights such as clone-specific programs and fate forecasting.

title: TetraCultures of Neurons, Astrocytes, Oligodendrocytes, and Microglia: A Murine In Vitro Model to Dissect Region-Specific CNS Immune Dynamics
summary:
Neuroinflammation and glial scar formation in the central nervous system (CNS) emerge from coordinated signaling between neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes and microglia. Conventional embryonic neuron-astrocyte-oligodendrocyte (NAO) TriCultures lack microglia and cannot model innate immune responses. Here, we introduce postnatal neuron-astrocyte-oligodendrocyte-microglia (NAOM) TetraCultures, in which resident microglia are retained from the original brain tissue and co-develop with other CNS cell populations from the onset of culture. Hippocampal and cortical cultures were maintained for 14 days in vitro and challenged with LPS, poly I or scratch injury.
  Only NAOM TetraCultures mounted robust, region- and stimulus-specific inflammatory responses. LPS induced marked TNF-αand IL-1βsecretion and increased IBA1 in hippocampal microglia, whereas poly I elicited IFN-βrelease without increasing IBA1. CD68 regulation differed between hippocampus and cortex, and microglial morphology showed pronounced amoeboid transitions after LPS. Astrocytes in NAOM TetraCultures expanded their territorial coverage after LPS, an effect absent in NAO TriCultures. Following scratch injury, IL-1βincreased, microglia infiltrated lesion zones and astrocytes formed lesion borders.
  Thus, NAOM TetraCultures recapitulate key features of CNS immunity, glial scar formation and region-specific glial responses while providing a physiologically relevant microglia-containing model.

AI.tldr: NAOM TetraCultures (neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and retained microglia) model CNS immunity, region-specific glial responses, and glial scar formation, unlike microglia-free TriCultures.
AI.motivation: Conventional NAO TriCultures lack microglia, so they cannot model innate immune responses or neuroinflammation and glial scar formation, which require coordinated signaling among neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia.
AI.method: Developed postnatal NAOM TetraCultures retaining resident microglia that co-develop with other CNS cells from culture onset. Maintained hippocampal and cortical cultures for 14 days in vitro and challenged them with LPS, poly I:C, or scratch injury.
AI.result: Only NAOM TetraCultures showed robust, region- and stimulus-specific inflammatory responses: LPS induced TNF-α and IL-1β secretion and increased IBA1 in hippocampal microglia; poly I:C elicited IFN-β without IBA1 increase. CD68 regulation differed by region, microglia became amoeboid after LPS, astrocytes expanded territorial coverage (absent in TriCultures), and after scratch injury IL-1β rose with microglial infiltration and astrocytic lesion borders.
AI.conclusion: NAOM TetraCultures recapitulate key features of CNS immunity, glial scar formation, and region-specific glial responses, offering a physiologically relevant microglia-containing model.

title: Calibrating AlphaFold confidence scores for interface quality
summary: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used to rank protein complex predictions and to select subsets of models for downstream applications. Although these scores provide strong discriminatory power for distinguishing prediction quality, their numerical values were never intended to represent the probability that a prediction satisfies a given structural quality criterion. In this work, we calibrate commonly used confidence scores to estimate the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen threshold of DockQ, an established measure of interface quality. On antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets, post-hoc isotonic calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving the underlying score ordering. The calibrated probabilities also provide more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a given structural quality threshold. Although the mapping is fitted within a given prediction distribution and therefore transfers imperfectly across prediction domains, we show that reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples. Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and requires no underlying AlphaFold model fine-tuning, it provides a straightforward and customizable way to convert existing model quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.

AI.tldr: AlphaFold confidence scores are calibrated post-hoc (via isotonic regression) to output the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a chosen DockQ threshold. Calibration improves probability agreement and selection estimates while preserving rankings, transferring imperfectly across domains but recoverable with few labeled samples.
AI.motivation: AlphaFold confidence scores are widely used for ranking and selecting protein complex predictions, and they discriminate quality well, but their numerical values were never meant to represent the probability that a prediction meets a given structural quality criterion. Users thus lack a principled probabilistic interpretation of these scores.
AI.method: Post-hoc isotonic calibration of commonly used AlphaFold confidence scores, mapping them to the probability that a predicted complex exceeds a selected DockQ threshold. Evaluated on antibody-antigen and general multimer datasets; the mapping is fitted within a prediction distribution and requires no AlphaFold fine-tuning.
AI.result: Calibration consistently improves agreement between predicted probabilities and observed DockQ success rates while preserving score ordering, and yields more accurate estimates of the fraction of selected models expected to pass a quality threshold. Cross-domain transfer is imperfect, but reliable estimates are recovered from a small number of labeled target-domain samples.
AI.conclusion: Because the calibration is entirely post hoc and needs no model fine-tuning, it offers a simple, customizable way to convert existing AlphaFold quality rankings into calibrated probabilities of passing a chosen structural quality threshold.

title: Probability generating functions for epidemiological time series
summary: Probability generating functions (PGFs) are a fundamental tool in mathematical epidemiology to characterize the stochastic evolution of epidemics via branching process theory. However, they are rarely used as operational tools in real-time during an outbreak, the main barrier being a lack of a systematic, computational methodology to describe epidemiological time series, such as cases or hospital admissions over time. Here, we introduce a general and computationally efficient framework for outbreak analytics based on PGFs. We first develop a method to encode joint distributions of incidences and their noisy measurements by realistic surveillance systems. Then, by transforming PGFs to cumulant generating functions (CGFs), we enable efficient evaluation of these joint distributions. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach for Bayesian inference and short-term forecasts, offering a significant computational advantage over simulation-based methods. Altogether, our framework operationalizes generating functions and paves the way for their broader adoption in computational epidemiology.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a general, computationally efficient framework based on probability generating functions (PGFs) for real-time outbreak analytics, enabling Bayesian inference and short-term forecasting more efficiently than simulation-based methods.
AI.motivation: PGFs are fundamental in mathematical epidemiology for characterizing stochastic epidemic evolution via branching process theory, but they are rarely used operationally in real-time during outbreaks. The main barrier is the lack of a systematic, computational methodology to describe epidemiological time series such as cases or hospital admissions over time.
AI.method: The authors develop a framework that (1) encodes joint distributions of incidences and their noisy measurements by realistic surveillance systems, and (2) transforms PGFs into cumulant generating functions (CGFs) to enable efficient evaluation of these joint distributions.
AI.result: The approach demonstrates practicality for Bayesian inference and short-term forecasts, offering a significant computational advantage over simulation-based methods.
AI.conclusion: The framework operationalizes generating functions and paves the way for their broader adoption in computational epidemiology.

title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks
summary: Subcellular signaling pathways regulating, e.g., cell division or synaptic plasticity, are often modeled as dynamical networks of reactions satisfying the law of mass action. To remain physically grounded, these models must satisfy different physical conservation laws, such as conservation of energy. This gives rise to thermodynamic constraints formalized by the Wegscheider conditions, which ensure that the system is in detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing Wegscheider conditions requires identifying cycles in the reaction network. This can become computationally cumbersome, especially in large, complex systems. Furthermore, even when these constraints are explicitly available, enforcing them requires choosing a reparameterization of the network, which may introduce asymmetries among the parameters and affect numerical conditioning. Moreover, this approach often causes inverse uncertainty quantification methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to struggle. Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in the parameter space, we propose an approach for promoting physical consistency by penalizing parameters that violate detailed balance. We first illustrate the approach on a simple reaction network containing a single cycle. We show that parameter values inferred without thermodynamic constraints can reproduce the experimental data seemingly accurately, while substantially violating the Wegscheider condition. In contrast, the proposed approach preserves the agreement with the observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. We further apply the approach to a model of PKA-calcineurin signaling in synaptic long-term depression, demonstrating its applicability to a more complex biochemical reaction network.

AI.tldr: A penalty-based method enforces thermodynamic constraints (Wegscheider/detailed balance) in mass-action reaction networks, avoiding explicit cycle enumeration and reparameterization, and works within MCMC for inverse uncertainty quantification.
AI.motivation: Subcellular signaling models as mass-action reaction networks must satisfy physical conservation laws (e.g., energy), formalized by Wegscheider conditions ensuring detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing these requires identifying network cycles—computationally cumbersome in large systems—and choosing a reparameterization that introduces parameter asymmetries and hurts numerical conditioning. This also causes MCMC-based inverse uncertainty quantification to struggle.
AI.method: Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in parameter space, the authors penalize parameters that violate detailed balance, promoting physical consistency without explicit cycle identification or reparameterization. Demonstrated first on a simple single-cycle reaction network, then applied to a PKA-calcineurin signaling model in synaptic long-term depression.
AI.result: In the simple network, unconstrained inference reproduces experimental data seemingly accurately but substantially violates the Wegscheider condition. The penalty approach preserves agreement with observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. Applicability is further shown on the complex PKA-calcineurin signaling network.
AI.conclusion: Penalizing detailed-balance violations offers a practical, scalable way to enforce thermodynamic consistency in dynamical reaction networks, avoiding the computational and numerical issues of explicit Wegscheider constraints, and is compatible with MCMC-based uncertainty quantification.

title: Model-Based Cortisol Replacement Strategies for Patients With Adrenal Insufficiency
summary: Cortisol is an essential hormone secreted by the adrenal glands. Abnormally low level of cortisol is referred to as adrenal insufficiency. This paper focuses on devising treatment strategies for patients suffering from adrenal insufficiency using a model-based approach. Two conditions of adrenal insufficiency are analysed. They are hypothalamic-pituitary (HP) and adrenal gland disorders. The hypothalamus, pituitary, and adrenal glands constitute the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which regulates stress and maintains physiological homeostasis through cortisol secretion. A comparative analysis of the existing mathematical models of the HPA axis is conducted. Based on this analysis, a novel model of the HPA axis is proposed that incorporates endogenous circadian rhythm. This proposed model is used to design effective cortisol replacement strategies. In addition, hydrocortisone replacement therapies are proposed and validated with clinical data from the literature. The results presented in this paper are applicable to patient-specific treatment strategies for individuals with adrenal insufficiency.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a novel mathematical model of the HPA axis incorporating endogenous circadian rhythm to design patient-specific cortisol replacement strategies for adrenal insufficiency.
AI.motivation: Adrenal insufficiency results from abnormally low cortisol. Effective treatment strategies are needed, and a model-based approach can help design cortisol replacement tailored to patients with HP or adrenal gland disorders.
AI.method: A comparative analysis of existing HPA axis models is conducted, followed by the proposal of a new HPA axis model with endogenous circadian rhythm. This model is used to design cortisol replacement strategies and hydrocortisone replacement therapies, validated with clinical data from the literature.
AI.result: The proposed model enables effective cortisol replacement strategies, and hydrocortisone replacement therapies are validated against clinical data.
AI.conclusion: The findings support patient-specific treatment strategies for individuals with adrenal insufficiency.

title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
summary: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect.
