AI.conclusion: The results support latent distribution transport as a principled and empirically effective formulation for perturbation-aware virtual cell modeling.

title: Beyond Discrimination: Evaluating Probability Calibration in Radiomics-Image Fusion for Renal Cell Carcinoma Classification
comment: 12 pages. 1 figure. Accepted at the 2026 Irish Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science (AICS 2026). Proceedings forthcoming
summary: Reliable probability estimates are important for the clinical interpretation of machine-learning classifiers, yet radiomics--image fusion models for renal cell carcinoma (RCC) are commonly evaluated primarily by discrimination. Using 396 patients from the KiTS23 dataset, we evaluated whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improved probabilistic performance in addition to discrimination. Seventeen individual models and four probability-average ensembles were assessed using discrimination, probability calibration, and proper scoring measures. Across 12 matched image-only versus fusion comparisons, AUC and AP improved in all 12, while Brier score and negative log likelihood (NLL) improved in 11 of 12 and expected calibration error (ECE) in eight of 12. The 3D MedVAE gated-fusion model achieved the strongest overall individual-model profile. Probability averaging across concatenation, cross-attention, and gated fusion produced favourable point estimates across all five primary metrics relative to image-only models in all four families, although paired-bootstrap support was stronger for Brier score and NLL than for ECE. These findings show that radiomics--image fusion can improve probabilistic prediction quality beyond discrimination, while calibration behaviour varies across image architectures and fusion strategies. We show that our proposed probability-average ensemble models improve discrimination and calibration simultaneously across all architectures in the study.

AI.tldr: Adding radiomics to image-based models for renal cell carcinoma improves not just discrimination but also probabilistic performance (calibration and scoring), with probability-average ensembles giving the best overall profile.
AI.motivation: Reliable probability estimates matter for clinical use of ML classifiers, but radiomics-image fusion models for RCC are usually judged mainly by discrimination (AUC/AP), ignoring calibration and probabilistic quality.
AI.method: Used 396 patients from KiTS23. Evaluated whether adding radiomics to four image-model families improved probabilistic performance alongside discrimination. Assessed 17 individual models and 4 probability-average ensembles using discrimination, calibration, and proper scoring measures across 12 matched image-only vs. fusion comparisons.
AI.result: AUC and AP improved in all 12 comparisons; Brier and NLL improved in 11/12; ECE in 8/12. The 3D MedVAE gated-fusion model had the strongest individual-model profile. Probability averaging (concatenation, cross-attention, gated fusion) gave favourable point estimates on all five metrics in all four families, with paired-bootstrap support stronger for Brier/NLL than ECE.
AI.conclusion: Radiomics-image fusion improves probabilistic prediction quality beyond discrimination, though calibration varies by architecture and fusion strategy. The proposed probability-average ensembles improve discrimination and calibration simultaneously across all architectures.

title: manylp: reproducible, exact, and batched linear programming for genome-scale dynamic flux balance analysis
summary: Dynamic flux balance analysis (dFBA) and its community, spatial and ensemble variants predict microbial metabolism by solving one linear program (LP) per species and time step, often 10^6 to 10^8 LPs per study. These LPs share their constraint matrix and objective and differ only in their bounds, yet general-purpose solvers treat each one independently, and GPU first-order solvers struggle with the degenerate, badly scaled matrices of genome-scale models. Moreover, metabolic optima are usually faces rather than vertices, so solvers return arbitrary flux vectors and dFBA predictions depend on the solver used. We present manylp, a batched solver for such bounds-parametric LP families that returns certified vertex solutions. Building on the bunching technique of stochastic programming, manylp caches optimal bases and certifies whole batches with one dense matrix product per basis on CPUs or GPUs; LPs outside the cached critical regions are re-solved by a warm-started lexicographic dual simplex, and new bases are propagated across the batch. Each LP is certified optimal and unique under a lexicographic flux rule, or infeasible, in independent double-precision arithmetic. On a genome-scale dFBA workload, manylp certified 47,889 LPs per second on a CPU, 12 to 33 times faster than HiGHS, Gurobi, FICO Xpress, GLPK and OR-Tools (32 processes), and reached 682,000 LPs per second on one GPU for community ensembles, needing 76 simplex solves for 94.6 million LPs. Integrated into the muODE simulator, it accelerated single trajectories 84-fold and 16-member ensembles 635-fold, and made adaptive Runge-Kutta integration affordable, reducing biomass errors 83-fold. Integrating 49 equally optimal flux policies in one batched run showed that alternative optima change predicted acetate 4.2-fold and shift community composition. manylp is open source: https://github.com/cumbof/manylp.

AI.tldr: manylp is a batched solver for bounds-parametric LP families in dynamic flux balance analysis that caches optimal bases and certifies batches via dense matrix products, achieving up to 682,000 LPs/s on GPU and large speedups in dFBA simulations.
AI.motivation: dFBA and its variants solve 10^6–10^8 LPs per study, sharing constraint matrices and objectives but differing only in bounds. General solvers treat each LP independently, GPU first-order solvers struggle with degenerate genome-scale matrices, and metabolic optima are faces rather than vertices, so arbitrary flux vectors make predictions solver-dependent.
AI.method: manylp builds on stochastic programming's bunching technique: it caches optimal bases and certifies whole batches with one dense matrix product per basis on CPU/GPU. LPs outside cached critical regions are re-solved by a warm-started lexicographic dual simplex, with new bases propagated across the batch. Each LP is certified optimal and unique under a lexicographic flux rule, or infeasible, in independent double-precision arithmetic.
AI.result: On genome-scale dFBA, manylp certified 47,889 LPs/s on CPU (12–33× faster than HiGHS, Gurobi, FICO Xpress, GLPK, OR-Tools) and 682,000 LPs/s on one GPU for community ensembles (76 simplex solves for 94.6M LPs). In muODE it accelerated single trajectories 84× and 16-member ensembles 635×, made adaptive Runge-Kutta affordable with 83× lower biomass errors, and showed alternative optima change acetate 4.2× and shift community composition.
AI.conclusion: manylp provides certified, solver-independent batched LP solutions by exploiting shared structure across bounds-parametric LP families, enabling fast and reproducible dFBA simulation. It is open source at https://github.com/cumbof/manylp.

title: Bayesian adaptive design for neural recruitment curves
summary: Nonlinear response models remain ubiquitous across disciplines with recruitment curves describing muscle response to neural stimulation. Conventional acquisition methods typically rely on static uniform sampling, requiring many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting designs such as ML-PEST forfeit accurate characterization of the overall curve. We present a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to propose stimuli that maximize information gain across the full recruitment curve. We additionally implement a focused acquisition method that can target arbitrary subset of curve parameters, which we use to evaluate and interpret our design. In simulations, our design outperforms uniform sampling in recovering threshold while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform. It likewise matches our threshold-focused acquisition, suggesting our design doesn't trade off threshold estimation for recovering the curve. We further show data collected using our design yields greater power when detecting a change in threshold in intervention studies. Our design proposes the next stimulus within 5 seconds, making it feasible for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) experiments. Finally, we validate our design in TMS experiments and provide a library for Python, called onMEP, for online acquisition of neural recruitment curves.

AI.tldr: A Bayesian adaptive design for acquiring neural recruitment curves maximizes information gain across the whole curve, matching threshold-hunting accuracy (ML-PEST) and uniform-sampling curve accuracy simultaneously, and is validated in TMS experiments with a Python library (onMEP).
AI.motivation: Recruitment curves (e.g., muscle response to neural stimulation) are widely used, but conventional static uniform sampling requires many stimuli, while adaptive threshold-hunting methods like ML-PEST sacrifice accurate characterization of the overall curve. There is a need for an acquisition method that is both sample-efficient and characterizes the full curve, while remaining fast enough for TMS experiments.
AI.method: The authors propose a Bayesian adaptive design that uses posterior uncertainty over curve parameters to select stimuli maximizing information gain across the full recruitment curve. They also implement a focused acquisition method targeting an arbitrary subset of curve parameters for evaluation/interpretation, and provide a Python library (onMEP) for online acquisition.
AI.result: In simulations, the design outperforms uniform sampling for threshold recovery while matching ML-PEST, and outperforms ML-PEST in predictive curve accuracy while matching uniform sampling. It matches threshold-focused acquisition, indicating no trade-off between threshold estimation and curve recovery. Data collected with the design yields greater power for detecting threshold changes in intervention studies. The next stimulus is proposed within 5 seconds, making it feasible for TMS. The design was validated in TMS experiments.
AI.conclusion: The proposed Bayesian adaptive design efficiently recovers both threshold and the full recruitment curve, outperforming or matching existing methods depending on the metric, and is practical for real-time TMS use as validated experimentally and supported by the released onMEP Python library.

title: Multi-Agent Learning of Reactive Strategies in Iterated Games
comment: 27 pages, 14 figures (12 pages + 3 figures main text; 15 pages + 11 figures Supplemental Material). Code: https://github.com/james-wolfe/reactive-learning
summary: Learning agents, whether humans or algorithms, adapt to one another rather than to a fixed environment. Selfish learning need not produce a good outcome for the group, especially when learners face a social dilemma. The iterated prisoner's dilemma (IPD) is the classical example, but it is usually studied in populations of agents who imitate successful strategies. Here, we instead study selfish gradient ascent learners on the two-dimensional space of reactive strategies. A reactive strategy is described by two continuous traits: reciprocity, the chance of cooperating after the co-player cooperates, and forgiveness, the chance of cooperating after the co-player defects. Each learner updates its strategy in the direction that most rapidly improves its payoff against all other learners, by an amount governed by its learning rate. We show that heterogeneity in learning rates can qualitatively change the long-term outcome: a population with uniform learning rates converges to always-defect (ALLD), whereas a population with variable learning rates approaches generous-tit-for-tat (GTFT), which produces nearly optimal collective payoffs. In simulations, every population passes through a transient state of minimal forgiveness, in which the distribution of reciprocity determines the outcome. Variable learning rates promote cooperation because slow learners preserve high reciprocity until the population reaches this state. We prove sufficient conditions on the distribution of reciprocity for convergence to ALLD or to tit-for-tat (TFT). Variable learning rates also allow cooperation to recover from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning. These results suggest that purely selfish and myopic learning can produce persistent cooperation provided the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates.

AI.tldr: Selfish gradient-ascent learners playing the iterated prisoner's dilemma converge to always-defect under uniform learning rates, but variable learning rates drive the population to generous-tit-for-tat and near-optimal collective payoffs.
AI.motivation: Agents adapt to each other rather than a fixed environment, and selfish learning need not benefit the group, especially in social dilemmas. The classic IPD is usually studied with imitative agents, leaving open how purely selfish gradient learners on continuous strategy spaces behave.
AI.method: The authors model selfish gradient-ascent learners on the 2D space of reactive strategies, parameterized by reciprocity (cooperate after cooperation) and forgiveness (cooperate after defection). Each learner moves in the direction of steepest payoff improvement against all others, scaled by its learning rate. They analyze uniform vs. variable learning rates across populations, run simulations, and prove convergence conditions on trait distributions.
AI.result: Uniform learning rates converge to always-defect, while variable learning rates approach generous-tit-for-tat with nearly optimal collective payoffs. All populations pass through a transient minimal-forgiveness state where the reciprocity distribution determines the outcome. Slow learners preserve high reciprocity until this state is reached. Sufficient conditions on the reciprocity distribution are proven for convergence to ALLD or tit-for-tat. Variable learning rates also enable recovery from perturbation, which is provably impossible under uniform learning.
AI.conclusion: Purely selfish and myopic learning can yield persistent cooperation if the population has intrinsic variability in learning rates. Heterogeneity in learning rates qualitatively changes long-term collective outcomes in the IPD.

title: Training-Data Extraction from Genomic Language Models
summary: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, exposing a direct route for studying training-sequence extraction through the generation interface. We present an output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 that selects convergent groups of repeated generations without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access during candidate selection. Recovered content is then scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Across 304 runs on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes, the attack yields 888 candidate clusters, of which 85 match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a cluster-level attack success rate of 9.57%. Final filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at the 500-bp threshold and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training-sequence regions, respectively. Within-category source-homology screening retains 11 of the 22 events at a 99% exclusion threshold and four at 98%, with the latter mapping to two reference regions. The results establish convergence among repeated nucleotide generations as a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments and characterize how recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.

AI.tldr: A black-box, output-only attack extracts long training segments from the Evo 2 genomic language model by selecting convergent repeated generations, achieving a 9.57% cluster-level success rate.
AI.motivation: Genomic language models generate long nucleotide continuations from short prefixes, offering a direct route to study training-sequence extraction. The goal is to test whether such extraction is possible without gradients, token likelihoods, or training-corpus access.
AI.method: An output-only black-box attack on Evo 2 selects convergent groups of repeated generations during candidate selection. Recovered content is scored by an evaluator combining aligned length, nucleotide identity, match multiplicity, and sequence complexity. Experiments run 304 times on Evo 2 7B with bacteriophage and plasmid prefixes.
AI.result: The attack yields 888 candidate clusters, 85 of which match training segments of at least 500 bp, giving a 9.57% cluster-level success rate. Filtering retains 22 uniquely matched extraction events at 500 bp and 15 at 1,000 bp, covering 14 and 7 distinct training regions. Source-homology screening retains 11 of 22 events at 99% exclusion and four at 98%, the latter mapping to two reference regions. Recovery depends on prefix length, cluster size, perplexity, early stopping, and sequence domains.
AI.conclusion: Convergence among repeated nucleotide generations is shown to be a practical output-only signal for recovering long training-sequence segments from genomic language models.

title: Hybrid Context Forests and Bilateral Viterbi Matching for 3D Rib Centerline Tracing in CT
summary:
Automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01-R12, L01-L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent-bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs. We present ribline, an open-source three-stage framework combining: (1) an automatically detected lung-apex and vertebral-midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis-aware azimuthal angle for point ordering along each rib; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U-Net; and (3) a global stage that decomposes the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigns rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refines curves via template recovery and normal-plane centering (RibSnake). On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training and 12 evaluation scans), our pipeline achieves a labeled Chamfer distance of 2.05 mm, labeled clDice of 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), and zero false-positive curves on the evaluation split, and 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 annotated scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation.
  Code: https://github.com/wq2012/ribline
  Pretrained Models: https://huggingface.co/collections/wq2012/ribline

AI.tldr: ribline is an open-source three-stage framework for automatic extraction and anatomical numbering (R01-R12, L01-L12) of all 24 rib centerlines in thoracic CT, achieving 2.05 mm labeled Chamfer distance and 97.2% labeling accuracy on the SCR benchmark.
AI.motivation: Automatic rib centerline extraction and numbering is essential for unfolded rib visualization, fracture detection, and surgical navigation, but remains challenging due to adjacent-bone confluence, calcified costal cartilage bridges, kyphotic pose variation, and partial visibility of terminal ribs.
AI.method: A three-stage pipeline: (1) automatic detection of a lung-apex and vertebral-midline coordinate frame with a kyphosis-aware azimuthal angle for point ordering; (2) a hybrid voxel detector fusing an anatomically anchored Semantic Context Forest (SCF) with a lightweight 3D U-Net; (3) a global stage decomposing the probability skeleton into candidate curves, assigning rib indices via a bilateral Viterbi dynamic program coupled across both hemithoraces, and refining curves via template recovery and normal-plane centering (RibSnake).
AI.result: On the Siemens Corporate Research 2 mm thoracic CT benchmark (47 training, 12 evaluation scans): labeled Chamfer distance 2.05 mm, labeled clDice 0.886 (3 mm) and 0.945 (4 mm), 97.2% labeling accuracy (278/286 ribs), zero false-positive curves; 3.64 mm (median 2.39 mm) with 91.8% labeling accuracy across all 59 scans (1,402 ribs) in 5-fold cross-validation.
AI.conclusion: ribline provides an accurate, robust open-source solution for full 24-rib centerline extraction and anatomical labeling in thoracic CT, with code and pretrained models publicly released.

title: MP-MNCA: Morphology-Prior Masked Neighbor Cross-Attention for Efficient Spatial Domain Identification
comment: Both authors contributed equally to this work
summary: Spatial transcriptomics jointly captures molecular state, tissue morphology, and spatial organization, yet spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, obscuring differences in convergence efficiency. We introduce MP-MNCA, a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework that preserves the full 3,000 dimensional highly-variable-gene representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, with histological similarity incorporated as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective. Across 12 heterogeneous human dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) sections, MP-MNCA is evaluated against established spatial-domain baselines using both convergence trajectories and epoch-wise spatial-domain visualizations. Our results show that MP-MNCA (i) reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in substantially fewer training epochs, as reflected quantitatively by convergence curves and qualitatively by progressive spatial grids, and (ii) maintains strong clustering quality, achieving a mean peak refined ARI of 0.546 versus 0.549 for the strongest baseline (STAIG), while attaining the highest mean refined NMI of 0.657 versus 0.640. Moreover, MP-MNCA outperforms STAIG on 7 of 12 sections in ARI and 11 of 12 in NMI, demonstrating faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.

AI.tldr: MP-MNCA is a morphology-prior masked neighbor cross-attention framework for spatial transcriptomics that converges faster than baselines while matching or exceeding clustering quality.
AI.motivation: Spatial-domain methods are typically compared only at late training checkpoints, which hides differences in convergence efficiency.
AI.method: MP-MNCA preserves the full 3,000-dimensional HVG representation while selectively routing molecular information across spatial neighbors, using histological similarity as a continuous attention prior under a self-supervised masked neighbor-contrastive objective.
AI.result: Evaluated on 12 DLPFC sections, MP-MNCA reaches coherent spatial-domain structure in far fewer epochs and achieves mean peak refined ARI 0.546 (vs 0.549 STAIG) and highest mean refined NMI 0.657 (vs 0.640). It beats STAIG on 7/12 sections in ARI and 11/12 in NMI.
AI.conclusion: MP-MNCA delivers faster convergence without sacrificing spatial-domain quality.

title: AutoNovo: Agentic Program Search Discovers Transferable Nucleic Acid Design Algorithms
comment: 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). Workshop: Agentic AI for Biological Discovery
summary: In-silico optimization of nucleic acids relies on predictive oracles that imperfectly capture biological function, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Recent studies have shown that not all designers generalize equally well to independent models. In this work, we use agentic program search to iteratively propose, execute, evaluate, and revise code for nucleic-acid designers. We describe the successful strategies used to prompt the search. AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean among the evaluated methods on 3/3 DNA-design tasks in terms of in-silico performance, and 6/6 transfer tasks in terms of independent models. The designers come from a family of discovered nucleic acid designers rather than a single universal best designer. We plan to release the resulting designers. These results are the first steps in creating nucleic acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, and thus improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology.

AI.tldr: This work uses agentic program search to auto-discover families of nucleic-acid sequence designers that generalize better across independent predictive models.
AI.motivation: In-silico nucleic acid optimization depends on imperfect predictive oracles, so sequences optimized against one model may exploit model-specific artifacts and fail to generalize to independent models. Not all designers generalize equally well.
AI.method: Agentic program search that iteratively proposes, executes, evaluates, and revises code for nucleic-acid designers, along with successful prompting strategies.
AI.result: AutoNovo designers achieved the best observed mean on 3/3 DNA-design tasks (in-silico performance) and 6/6 transfer tasks (independent models). Best designers came from a family of discovered designers, not a single universal one.
AI.conclusion: These are first steps toward nucleic-acid designers that maximize cross-model generalization, improving the odds that in-silico designed sequences reflect real biology. The resulting designers will be released.

title: From Simulated Fluids to Living Tissue: Zero-Shot Foundation Model Transfer to Perturbed Embryos
summary:
Morphogenesis is driven by the interplay of genetic regulation and tissue mechanics. In vivo video data is limited, particularly under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond the most representative conditions in the dataset challenging. However, at tissue scales, the dynamics of Drosophila can be described as a continuum flow, motivating the usage of representations learned across other physical systems as priors for developmental dynamics.
  We investigate finetuning Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained across a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. We evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations. Zero-shot refers to evaluation on perturbation conditions never seen during wild-type finetuning, without any additional training. In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator model trained from scratch achieves best performance on VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift of unseen samples of mutated embryos and temperature conditions. Interestingly, predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone of embryo development.
  Our results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. More broadly, our results motivate further study of physics foundation models as a new complementary tool for the simulation of morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

AI.tldr: Finetuning Walrus, a continuum dynamics foundation model, on just 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos enables autoregressive tissue velocity prediction that generalizes best (CRPS) under severe distribution shifts from unseen mutations and temperatures, though a from-scratch FNO wins in-distribution (VRMSE).
AI.motivation: In vivo morphogenesis video data is limited, especially under genetic mutations and environmental perturbations, making generalization beyond representative dataset conditions hard. Since Drosophila tissue dynamics admit a continuum flow description at tissue scales, priors learned from other physical systems could serve as representations for developmental dynamics.
AI.method: Finetune Walrus, a Continuum Dynamics Foundation Model pretrained on a broad set of simulated continuous systems, on tissue velocity fields from only 12 wild-type Drosophila blastoderm videos. Evaluate autoregressive prediction both in-distribution and zero-shot under unseen temperature and genetic perturbations (no additional training).
AI.result: In-distribution, a Fourier Neural Operator trained from scratch achieves the best VRMSE. However, Walrus (CRPS) is the strongest model under the most severe distribution shift (unseen mutated embryos and temperature conditions). Predictions capture the shape of the mean surface tissue velocity trajectory and its separation between 17°C and 27°C, including the timing of the peak at Germ Band Extension onset, a biologically meaningful milestone.
AI.conclusion: Results provide preliminary support that representations learned from different dynamical systems can transfer to experimental morphogenesis in developmental regimes, provided they admit a continuum description. This motivates further study of physics foundation models as a complementary tool for simulating morphogenesis in low-data regimes.

title: CellChain: Benchmarking Cross-Scale Evidence Use for Perturbation Reasoning
summary: Recent advances in foundation models and large-scale cellular perturbation datasets have driven growing interest in using LLMs to predict and reason about cellular responses. Biological reasoning in this setting involves relating molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluating foundation models therefore requires assessing not only whether their predictions are correct, but also how those predictions depend on the biological evidence provided. We introduce CellChain, an experimentally grounded benchmark comprising 590 biological cases and 2,360 matched evidence-condition instances across gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. CellChain links perturbation experiments and external biological resources through a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while preserving questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules. Across 18 foundation models, the highest accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%, respectively, and broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. On the drug-sensitivity benchmark cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by an average of 13.0 percentage points in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis separates corrections, newly introduced errors, and wrong-answer switches, revealing substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences. CellChain provides controlled comparisons for attributing changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context, including changes in evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment.

AI.tldr: CellChain is an experimentally grounded benchmark (590 cases, 2,360 evidence-condition instances) for evaluating how LLM/foundation model predictions in cellular response reasoning depend on biological evidence, not just correctness.
AI.motivation: Foundation models and large-scale perturbation datasets are increasingly used to predict cellular responses, but such biological reasoning spans molecular mechanisms, cellular responses, and functional outcomes across scales. Evaluation must therefore assess not only whether predictions are correct but also how predictions depend on the biological evidence provided.
AI.method: CellChain covers gene-dependency prediction, cytokine-axis identification, and drug-sensitivity ranking. It links perturbation experiments with external biological resources via a provenance-aware evidence graph spanning molecular, pathway, transcriptional, and phenotypic information. Task-specific conditions vary evidence coverage, composition, or assignment while holding questions, candidate answers, reference targets, and scoring rules fixed. Evaluation spans 18 foundation models with decision-transition analysis.
AI.result: Best accuracies under prespecified target-evidence conditions are 57.5%, 75.5%, and 70.8%. Broader evidence coverage does not consistently improve accuracy. In the drug-sensitivity cohort, matched reference histories outperform swapped histories by 13.0 percentage points average in cluster-weighted accuracy. Decision-transition analysis reveals substantial answer changes hidden by small net accuracy differences.
AI.conclusion: CellChain enables controlled comparisons that attribute changes in model predictions to prespecified expansions of biological context (evidence coverage, composition, and biological assignment), offering a rigorous framework for evidence-aware evaluation of biological reasoning in foundation models.

title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
summary: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.

AI.tldr: The paper explores how molecular composition of complex natural odor mixtures relates to perceived similarity, using LLMs to derive scalable perceptual descriptions from a database of 1,200+ food odor mixtures with 8,000+ molecular components.
AI.motivation: Odor chemistry-perception relationships remain poorly understood. Most studies focus on single molecules, but natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding complexity to percept formation that prior work fails to address.
AI.method: Used a database of 1,200+ volatile-compound-in-food mixtures (8,000+ components). Employed LLMs as a scalable surrogate to derive mixture-level perceptual descriptions. Trained models to predict held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition via low-rank molecular embeddings, and compared against component-overlap metrics and external molecular features.
AI.result: Language-derived representations effectively supervised prediction of held-out mixture similarities. Prediction was strongest with chemosensory prompts. Learned low-rank molecular embeddings outperformed component-overlap metrics, even for mixtures with no shared molecules, and aligned with independent human odor-descriptor space despite no single-molecule labels. External molecular features showed modest zero-shot alignment and helped only under limited supervision.
AI.conclusion: Language-derived descriptions provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, advancing quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.

title: Beyond Successful Play: Diagnosing Opponent Modeling in Large Language Models
summary: Language-model agents are expected to adapt to others whose behavior changes through interaction. Yet adaptation may rely on learned behavioral patterns rather than theory of mind (ToM): the ability to infer others' mental states, including beliefs and intentions. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic framework for repeated hide-and-seek against algorithmic opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates. Their ground-truth beliefs and action probabilities let us distinguish adaptive play, action prediction, and belief tracking through live interaction, fixed-history evaluation, and controlled information interventions. With structured elicitation and behavioral supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we find improved play in several tested settings, but diagnostics reveal limitations in opponent prediction and belief tracking. We test whether supervising opponent action probabilities can address this predictive deficit in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Predictions improve when the model is told the opponent's type and parameter settings, but become less accurate when it must infer the opponent from history without this information. Training on examples that also omit these details reduces the gap, although improvements vary across opponents. Is this limitation specific to smaller open-weight models, or does it also appear in a frontier model? GPT-5.4 also benefits from correct opponent beliefs: supplying them improves its predictions and choices, whereas deeper explicit belief reports and self-generated memory do not consistently improve forecasting from interaction history. This contrast suggests that using useful belief information is easier than inferring it autonomously, even for a frontier model. Together, our findings distinguish improved play and action prediction from reliable belief tracking, providing a framework for evaluating mentalizing and testing targeted improvements.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a benchmark and diagnostic framework using repeated hide-and-seek against opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates, to disentangle adaptive play, action prediction, and belief tracking in LM agents. Findings show that even after structured elicitation and SFT improvements, opponent prediction and belief tracking remain limited, and that using belief information is easier than inferring it autonomously, even for a frontier model.
AI.motivation: Language-model agents are expected to adapt to opponents whose behavior changes through interaction, but observed adaptation may stem from learned behavioral patterns rather than genuine theory of mind (ToM)—the ability to infer others' beliefs and intentions. The paper seeks to distinguish true mentalizing from surface-level adaptive play and to diagnose where LM agents actually fail.
AI.method: A benchmark and diagnostic framework for repeated hide-and-seek against algorithmic opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates, providing ground-truth beliefs and action probabilities. The framework combines live interaction, fixed-history evaluation, and controlled information interventions to separate adaptive play, action prediction, and belief tracking. The authors use structured elicitation and behavioral supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and test whether supervising opponent action probabilities addresses predictive deficits (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct). They also test GPT-5.4 with correct opponent beliefs, explicit belief reports, and self-generated memory.
AI.result: Structured elicitation and behavioral SFT improve play in several settings, but diagnostics reveal persistent weaknesses in opponent prediction and belief tracking. For Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, predicting opponent actions improves when the model is told the opponent's type and parameters, but degrades when it must infer the opponent from history alone; training on examples omitting these details narrows the gap, though improvements vary across opponents. GPT-5.4 also benefits from being supplied correct opponent beliefs (improving predictions and choices), yet deeper explicit belief reports and self-generated memory do not consistently improve forecasting from interaction history.
AI.conclusion: Using useful belief information is easier than inferring it autonomously, even for a frontier model. The findings distinguish improved play and action prediction from reliable belief tracking, offering a framework for evaluating mentalizing and testing targeted improvements in language-model agents.

title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
comment: Experiment one presented at the 48th Annual Meeting of the Cognitive Science Society as a full paper talk in "Collective Intelligence."
summary: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

AI.tldr: A reservoir computing model shows interaction (pooled-feedback coupling) yields a dyadic advantage and better efficiency in collective decisions, unlike simple aggregation of independent responses.
AI.motivation: Wisdom-of-crowds aggregation usually improves performance, but interaction can sometimes harm groups. It remains unclear when and why interaction enhances joint performance in accuracy and efficiency, motivating a formal model.
AI.method: Echo state networks (reservoir computing) were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings, then tested in pairs and larger groups both with and without coupled pooled feedback.
AI.result: Interacting model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage of Bahrami et al. (2010), whereas aggregating independent responses did not. Aggregated outputs tended to diverge from runaway feedback, while interaction benefited dynamics. Larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models at equal total computation.
AI.conclusion: The model offers a formal framework explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence, highlighting accuracy and efficiency gains from coupled feedback.

title: MedEvo: Medical Reasoning Evolution through Knowledge Navigation
summary: Medical multimodal reasoning models are typically trained on teacher-generated rationales, discarding the valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories, while general-domain correction methods offer little guidance for errors in image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis. We propose MedEvo, which uses medical knowledge, namely a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis, to navigate both trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor locates the first consequential error and provides a minimal, answer-free hint; the same student retains the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, MedEvo identifies capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set and prioritizes related questions for new rollouts and repairs. With supervised fine-tuning (SFT) alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on the multimodal track of MedXpertQA (MedXpertQA-MM)), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B and Qwen3.5-397B mean accuracy from 67.91% to 73.04% and from 71.83% to 74.95%, respectively. Our analyses show that failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving, that repair success does not imply learning value, and that independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

AI.tldr: MedEvo is a framework that leverages medical knowledge (tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis) to repair failed reasoning trajectories and select training data, improving medical multimodal reasoning accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing medical multimodal reasoning models are trained on teacher-generated rationales, which discard valid reasoning in students' own failed trajectories. General-domain correction methods offer little guidance for medical-specific errors like image reading, anatomical context, or differential diagnosis.
AI.method: MedEvo uses a tag taxonomy and error-type diagnosis to guide trajectory repair and data selection. For each failed rollout, a gold-blind auditor finds the first consequential error and gives a minimal, answer-free hint; the student keeps the valid prefix and regenerates the erroneous suffix. After each round, capability gaps across medical tags on a held-out feedback set are identified, and related questions are prioritized for new rollouts and repairs.
AI.result: With SFT alone, MedEvo raises Qwen3.5-9B mean accuracy across seven benchmarks from 65.57% to 69.12% (47.40% to 54.50% on MedXpertQA-MM), surpassing teacher-distillation SFT (66.93%). It also raises Qwen3.5-35B from 67.91% to 73.04% and Qwen3.5-397B from 71.83% to 74.95%.
AI.conclusion: Failed trajectories contain reasoning worth preserving; repair success does not imply learning value; independent feedback is key to sustained improvement.

title: Understanding Gene Expression-to-Image Learning: Spatial Structure and Information Fidelity
summary: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables cell-level analysis of biological heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles remains challenging. Gene Expression-to-Image (GE2I) offers an effective learning strategy by arranging gene values on pixel grids for convolutional neural networks, but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear. We study GE2I on full-transcriptome data while keeping the network and training procedure fixed. Our results reveal a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity. Structured mappings produce smooth, low-frequency patterns that support faster early optimization, whereas assigning multiple genes to the same pixel obscures expression differences and can reduce predictive performance. This trade-off explains why random mappings can compete with structured layouts when many genes are represented. One-to-one gene-to-pixel assignment improves prediction across the tested visual backbones even when image smoothness decreases. We further find that the benefits of pretraining and augmentation depend on the backbone and mapping. These findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation and the transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates GE2I, mapping gene expression onto pixel grids for CNNs, revealing a trade-off between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity that guides better gene-to-pixel assignment.
AI.motivation: scRNA-seq enables cell-level analysis of heterogeneity, but learning effective representations from high-dimensional, unordered gene expression profiles is difficult. GE2I offers an effective learning strategy but its underlying mechanisms remain unclear.
AI.method: Study GE2I on full-transcriptome data with fixed network and training procedure; analyze structured vs. random mappings and gene-to-pixel assignment (one-to-one vs. many-to-one) across visual backbones.
AI.result: A trade-off emerges between spatial smoothness and gene-level fidelity: structured mappings yield smooth low-frequency patterns aiding faster early optimization, while multiple genes per pixel obscure differences and can hurt prediction. One-to-one assignment improves prediction across backbones even with lower smoothness. Pretraining and augmentation benefits depend on backbone and mapping.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide practical guidance for pixel allocation, explaining why random mappings can compete with structured ones, and inform transfer of vision priors to gene expression data.

title: ECG-RSI: Recursive Self-Improvement through Targeted Electrocardiogram Waveform Evolution
summary: Electrocardiogram (ECG) models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and remains faithful to waveform evidence. We introduce ECG-RSI, a recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set. Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean question-answering accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. Across the retained trajectory, the preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts. Continued feedback correction yields diminishing external gains. These results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and checking whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: ECG-RSI is a recursive self-improvement framework for ECG models that combines verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search, improving QA accuracy and classification F1 on seven benchmarks.
AI.motivation: ECG models need supervision that targets evolving weaknesses and stays faithful to waveform evidence. Static supervision cannot keep pace with changing model weaknesses or ensure evidence-grounded answers.
AI.method: A recursive self-improvement framework combining verified waveform synthesis with feedback-guided intervention search. Signal remeasurement verifies waveform edits; construction errors guide generator repair, while learner errors motivate interventions compared on a separate selection set.
AI.result: Across seven benchmarks, three rounds raise Qwen3.5-35B-A3B's mean QA accuracy from 34.57% to 56.04% and mean classification F1 from 24.27 to 34.03. The preferred supervision shifts from direct reinforcement to confusion-focused contrasts, with diminishing external gains from continued feedback correction.
AI.conclusion: Results motivate separating error diagnosis from intervention selection and verifying whether gains on the feedback set transfer to independent benchmarks.

title: Spatial Kernel Restricted Canonical Correlation Analysis: Population Targets, Identifiability, and Stability
summary: Relating observations of different categories across space requires methods that accommodate distinct sampling locations and spatial dependence. Spatial kernel restricted canonical correlation analysis (skrCCA) uses spatial weights to identify associated feature combinations across data categories. Here, we develop a statistical theory of its covariance form after feature reduction. Conditional on the observed locations and under a mean-zero model, the pairwise association matrices target kernel-weighted averages of cross-covariances. For prespecified directions, we derive the exact null variance under independence between blocks. We establish recovery and stability bounds in two- and multiblock settings under explicit population models, and show that exact cyclic updates have convergent objective values. The variance characterization shows how spatial weighting and within-block dependence jointly determine the effective information available for estimating association. The recovery bounds separate statistical and optimization error, relating stability to population separation and the strength of connections between blocks. These results clarify what fitted spatial association axes estimate and provide conditions under which they can be recovered reliably.

AI.tldr: This paper develops a statistical theory for spatial kernel restricted canonical correlation analysis (skrCCA), characterizing the covariance form after feature reduction and establishing recovery, stability, and convergence guarantees.
AI.motivation: Relating observations across spatial categories requires methods handling distinct sampling locations and spatial dependence. skrCCA addresses this via spatial weights, but its statistical properties lacked theoretical grounding.
AI.method: Under a mean-zero model conditional on observed locations, the authors analyze the covariance form of skrCCA after feature reduction, deriving exact null variance for prespecified directions under block independence, and establishing recovery and stability bounds in two- and multiblock settings, plus convergence of exact cyclic updates.
AI.result: Pairwise association matrices target kernel-weighted averages of cross-covariances. Variance characterization shows spatial weighting and within-block dependence jointly determine effective information. Recovery bounds separate statistical and optimization error; exact cyclic updates have convergent objective values.
AI.conclusion: The results clarify what fitted spatial association axes estimate and give conditions under which they can be reliably recovered.

title: Lossless Reductions and Hybrid Sampling for Phylogeny Using the Maximum Compatibility Criterion
summary:
Maximum compatibility provides a criterion for phylogenetic reconstruction in which the objective is to retain a maximum set of mutually compatible characters. For binary characters, pairwise compatibility can be represented by a weighted graph whose vertices correspond to characters and whose edges connect compatible pairs. A leading algorithm by Cherry [BMC Bioinformatics, 18(1):127, 2017] uses this representation to identify maximum compatible character sets as maximum weight cliques.
  We formulate the problem as maximum weight independent set enumeration on the complement graph and use deterministic postprocessing to map sampled bit strings to maximal feasible solutions. To explore the prospects of quantum computational advantage, we further construct bespoke correction-in-the-loop Quantum Approximate Optimisation Algorithm instances and find that traditional Lagrange multiplier choices may not be optimal for the enumeration problem on noisy devices.
  We also introduce lossless graph reductions with reconstruction rules that preserve the complete set of optimal solutions. Our results indicate that graph reduction and sampling can be effectively combined to address the enumeration bottleneck in maximum compatibility phylogeny, while retaining exact reconstruction when the residual optimum set is completely resolved.
  We enhance Cherry's approach to maximum compatibility by introducing graph reduction techniques and quantum sampling. title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
comment: Accepted at IWAI 2026, forthcoming in the Springer proceedings. 17 pages: the 13-page camera-ready paper, reproduced without alteration apart from one typographical fix, followed by 4 pages of supplementary material. summary: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.

AI.tldr: The paper compares two ways an active-inference agent can prioritise an urgent bodily need—sharpening interoceptive precision vs. reweighting outcome preferences—showing they trade off between survival, the learned body model's coverage and quality.
AI.motivation: Embodied agents face competing bodily needs, and it is unclear how the mechanism used to prioritise a need (precision vs. preference) affects survival, perception, and the body model learned.
AI.method: In a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, the authors separately and jointly test two interventions: increasing precision of interoceptive information about an urgent need, and increasing preference for need-relieving outcomes. They also run an experiment on 72 additional layouts.
AI.result: Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states farther from lethal boundaries and shifts the states the agent learns from, yielding a learned model with narrower coverage, lower quality overall but slightly higher quality at visited levels. On difficult layouts the predicted preference benefit is not confirmed, though both interventions raise average survival and their interaction is positive.
AI.conclusion: Survival alone is an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body; perception and model quality must be considered.

title: MFG: Multi-turn Feedback Guided Molecular Optimization
summary: Multi-objective molecular optimization is a critical process in drug discovery that aims to modify a given molecule to simultaneously improve multiple properties while maintaining a similar overall structure. This process often requires iterative modifications guided by computational or experimental feedback. Recent large language model (LLM)-based methods have begun to explore this iterative approach; however, these methods are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback, while existing approaches primarily focus on single-turn molecular optimization. To address this gap, we introduce Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. MFG introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, alongside a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. We apply MFG over $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$, a state-of-the-art LLM model for multi-objective molecular optimization, evaluate $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ on ten multi-objective molecular optimization tasks. The results demonstrate that $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O-MFG}$ achieves the highest average similarity-constrained success rate ($81.50%$), outperforming the base model $\text{GeLLM}^{3}\text{O}$ ($70.81%$).

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Multi-turn Feedback Guided (MFG) molecular optimization, a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM (GeLLM³O) to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns, achieving an 81.50% success rate.

While recent LLM-based methods explore this iterative approach, they are not explicitly trained to leverage such feedback and mostly focus on single-turn optimization.
AI.method: MFG is a reinforcement learning framework that trains an LLM to progressively optimize molecules using feedback from previous turns. It introduces a feedback vector capturing both property improvements and source molecule similarity, along with a feedback-aligned reward function that promotes progressive improvement across turns. It is applied over GeLLM³O.

AI.conclusion: MFG effectively enhances LLMs for multi-turn molecular optimization, yielding a significant improvement in success rate over the base model.
